How bank secrecy began as a shield against the Nazis

footnote.text: You have to do your KYC afresh every year.

brief.head: Firms have secrets too
brief.text: A firm’s list of customers and vendors, handed to rivals or the powerful, could destroy it, Ajay Shah said: “It’s like a death sentence.” {074-C02}

brief.head: Walls, then thoughts
brief.text: Privacy was not always ours, Amit Varma said: thicker walls and separate bedrooms gave people a rich interior life. “You’re not alone if you know you’re being watched.” {074-C05}

brief.head: Lose one, lose both
brief.text: Trading freedom for security is a false bargain, Amit Varma argued, since freedom given to the state removes your security against it. “So actually we lose both.” {074-C09}

brief.head: Who funds the club?
brief.text: Freedom of association rests on financial privacy, Ajay Shah said. If the state sees who funds an organisation, the powerful can go after its funders. {074-C03}

brief.head: Not just theatre
brief.text: Airport checks are security theatre, Ajay Shah said, but financial surveillance is a public-choice grab: “they grab power over the people under the excuse of terrorism.” {074-C08}

thought.text: Freedom is the world of not being observed.
thought.who: Ajay Shah, making the case that financial privacy is personal privacy

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on India’s paperwork ordeal
lead.head: Prove you exist. Again. Every year
body: Amit Varma opened the episode by doubting that his co-host was his co-host. “Bearded economists look alike to me,” he said. “Prove to me that you’re Ajay Shah. Kaagaz dikhaao!” {074-J01}
Shah had no papers and offered his face instead. The joke set up an episode on KYC, the know-your-customer checks Indian banks keep running.
Shah’s own bank asks him every year to prove again that he is who he said he was. Accounts with money in them, he said, get frozen when KYC goes wrong.
For the privileged, who can march up to the bank manager, it is a nuisance. For most Indians, Shah said, “this is just a living nightmare”.
## Privacy is privacy
Shah began with first principles. A spy who follows a person learns what she says, does and buys; a complete view of her finances, he argued, reveals as much.
The proposition, he said, was simple: “if you believe in personal privacy, you should equally believe in financial privacy.” {074-C01}

The retort “if you have nothing to hide” misses the point. People who know they are watched bend their behaviour to suit the watcher. “A world in which you do not have privacy is not freedom,” Shah said.
His model is the wiretap. In liberal democracies a police officer must convince a judge with prima facie evidence, the tap lasts a finite time, and nobody runs mass surveillance of everyone’s phone.

Shah wants the same for money: customers able to tell their bank to delete transactions after three days, and police needing a warrant to watch a suspect for a fixed period. “It is only in a police state that a policeman’s job is easy,” he said. {074-C04}
## A slow creep

The history, as Shah told it, is a slow creep. In 1933 Nazi Germany made its citizens disclose their overseas assets. In the 1970s American banks had to report large transactions to the tax authorities, and nobody objected, because it was only about tax evaders.
Richard Nixon’s war on drugs created the crime of money laundering, and a club of countries, FATF, grew around it. After the 9/11 attacks the US Treasury pushed its rules on the world.
## The world’s worst

Shah disagrees with the FATF rules even in rich countries, but in London, Zurich or Washington opening a bank account involves little misery. In India each layer makes them worse: the government’s rules, then the RBI, then the bank, then the frontline employee.
No one answers for the welfare of citizens. Each, Shah said, is thinking: “My only objective is to cover my ass.” {074-C10}
The poor and small firms give up and fall back on cash, gold and real estate.
Shah also confessed that he had once believed Aadhaar would fix all this. “And in hindsight I realize how wrong it was,” he said. {074-S07}
The first Aadhaar number was issued in 2009, yet banks still demand fresh KYC every year. “CPUs are never the answer,” Shah said.

His larger lesson was to be sceptical of “global best practice”. Policies that seem to work in America rest there on invisible supports: liberal democracy, courts, checks and balances, norms. It was “stupid in India to accept this”, he said.
Varma’s song of the day was *Every Breath You Take* by The Police. Shah’s advice: “Please email this to all the civil servants in your life.”

second.label: Terror finance
second.head: The 555 loophole
second.deck: Ajay Shah on why following the money after 9/11 never stopped terror plots
body: After the 9/11 attacks, the idea took hold that terror plots could be caught by finding the $100,000 wired by a Pakistani major general to Mohammed Atta, who organised the attacks. Ajay Shah called it “not a very bright idea”.

His counterexample is a 555 cigarette box packed with diamonds, which holds about $100,000 and is invisible to X-ray machines. {074-C07} He wondered aloud how modern machines would see it. Monitor seven billion people, he said, and terrorists simply move to other channels. {#sevenbillion}
By now, Shah said, it is well known that the system has not disrupted terror plots. It has only fouled up finance and given governments more information about their subjects.

quote.text: You want to move a hundred thousand dollars to Mohammed Atta, you just have to carry one cigarette case.

second.caption: the cigarette box of diamonds

third.head: Cruelty by paperwork
body: A very smart friend of Amit Varma’s, in her 40s, had a supplementary credit card linked to her husband’s. She had done her KYC the year before, but this year she could not get through the paperwork in time. She lost the card; he kept his. {074-S03}
Varma also remembered his father in his last years, unable to cope. “It was cruelty,” he said, “to expect a man of advancing years or a woman of advancing years to deal with all of this.”
Even Harsh Vardhan, a senior banking figure who knows the people who run the banks, told Varma what a nightmare his own KYC had been: phone calls here, phone calls there. {074-S02}
Poor people and small firms, Ajay Shah said, “just look at all this and they give up”.
third.caption: the paperwork maze

p2.title: Know your citizen
p2.deck: Ajay Shah’s case for financial privacy, and how India came to have the world’s worst KYC

sections.label: The first principle
sections.head: Your wallet is your diary
sections.caption: financial privacy as personal privacy
body: Ajay Shah went back to fundamentals: what is the case for financial privacy? A spy who follows a person learns what she says, does and buys, and in a liberal democracy that is not on. A full picture of her finances, he argued, reveals as much. {074-C01}

The reply “if you have nothing to hide” misses the point. Once you know you are being observed, Shah said, you are in the panopticon, and your days are distorted “out of deference to the watcher”. {#chillingeffect}
Amit Varma challenged anyone who uses that argument to make their Google searches public. {#incognito} “What do you do in the Chrome incognito window?” he asked.
## Firms and funders

Shah extended the case to companies. Populism, he said, grants individuals some privacy but treats firms as fair game. Yet a firm’s customers and vendors can be read from its financial statements, and that list in hostile hands could destroy it. {074-C02}

Privacy also underpins freedom of association, the right to form clubs, parties, NGOs and companies. If the state can see who funds an organisation, the powerful can go after its funders. {074-C03} Varma’s example: a ruling party could order a tax raid on someone donating to the opposition.

~ Varma, drawing on his conversation with Rahul Matthan, added that privacy is a historical achievement. Thicker walls and separate bedrooms gave people the solitude in which a rich interior life could grow.

quote.text: Then if you will shatter financial privacy, you have shattered right to association.

sections.label: The backstory
sections.head: A Nazi idea goes global
sections.caption: the history of financial surveillance
body: Banks once kept their customers’ affairs private by an informal code, Ajay Shah said. The break came in 1933, when Nazi Germany required every citizen to disclose their overseas assets. Governments all over the world now do the same. “We have normalized oppression in the modern world,” he said. {074-C06}

The American creep began with the tax authorities. In the 1970s banks had to report transactions above ten thousand dollars to the IRS, and nobody spoke up, because it was only about tax evaders. {#tenthousand}

Richard Nixon’s war on drugs then created the crime of money laundering, and the Financial Action Task Force grew around it. The US law, Shah said, was called the Banking Privacy Act: “It is actually the destruction of privacy in Banking Act.” {#orwell}
## Join, or else
FATF is a closed club of major countries, and India, Shah said, was its last member. Others faced a choice: sign up to financial surveillance or face more friction in the world. {074-R19}
After the 9/11 attacks, the US Treasury championed AML-CFT, anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terror, across the world.
~ By now, Shah said, it is well known that none of this has disrupted terror plots. It has fouled up finance and handed governments more information about their subjects.

quote.text: And the slippery slope began. And then it started getting worse and it started getting worse.

sections.label: India’s version
sections.head: Worse, worse, worst
sections.caption: why India’s KYC is the worst
body: Ajay Shah disagrees with the FATF rules even in rich countries. But open a bank account in London, Zurich or Washington, he said, and your level of misery is low, like an airport check that “may be stupid, but it’s not so bad”. {#londonzurich}

In India the same rules pass through layer after layer. The government writes their harshest version into its rules. The RBI, Shah said, “will make something worse out of it”. {#rbi} The bank does the same, and the frontline employee interprets it in the worst possible way.
No one at any step answers for the welfare of citizens. Each, in Shah’s telling, is thinking: “My only objective is to cover my ass.” {074-C10}
## The cost
The heaviest burden falls on the poor, who lack the time and the ability to fight through the complexity. Poor people and small firms give up, and financial exclusion follows.
It has become harder and harder, Shah said, to run a firm of five, ten, twenty or forty people in India. {#smallfirms}
~ Meanwhile, he said, “all of us just roll our eyes and get miserable and put up one sentence on Twitter and let it go”.

quote.text: So each one comes up with a harder and crazier version of it.

sections.label: The mea culpa
sections.head: Chips won’t fix the state
sections.caption: why Aadhaar didn’t end KYC
body: Ajay Shah owned up to an error. People in finance, himself included, had thought Aadhaar would provide an end run around the KYC mess. “I am guilty,” he said. “I’m part of this thought process.” {074-S07}

Aadhaar was supposed to make the problem mysteriously vanish, he said, because his iris scan does not change through his life. Yet the first Aadhaar number was given out in 2009, and in 2024 his bank still tells him to do his KYC afresh every year. {#aadhaar2009}
His general law: “Adding CPUs to a malfunctioning Indian government never makes the Indian government better.” {074-C11} You have to go deep inside, he said, and fix the organisation.
## The perfect and the good

Amit Varma, not wanting the perfect to be the enemy of the good, asked why a simple central directive could not declare that Aadhaar suffices. Shah answered with public choice theory. Officials who want to cover themselves will keep coming up with one more rule, so “the idea that good sense will prevail is the flaw”.
~ The fix, he said, lies at the root cause, in “the hard work of humanities and liberal arts”. {#humanities}

quote.text: So trying to find an end run around problems of public administration with a technological silver bullet, that is the core flaw.

sections.label: The lesson
sections.head: Handle imports with care
sections.caption: global best practice
body: What would a good future look like, Amit Varma asked. Ajay Shah wants constitutional law and the courts to shut down all mass surveillance in finance, building on the Puttaswamy ruling and the right to association. {#courts}

A customer should be able to tell a bank to delete every transaction “one millisecond after they take place”. Police who have proved that someone is a drug dealer should get a warrant from something like an American FISA court, and then see that person’s transactions for 90 days. {#ninetydays}
## Invisible infrastructure
The wider lesson, which Shah traced to Lant Pritchett and to Kelkar and Shah, is to be sceptical of “global best practice”. {#pritchett}

A policy that seems to work in the United States rests there on supports nobody sees: liberal democracy, checks and balances, courts, communities and norms. Naively transplanted into India, Shah argued, it does far worse. {074-C12}
~ It was “wrong and dangerous and evil”, he said, for the US Treasury to push financial surveillance all over the world, “and it was stupid in India to accept this”.

quote.text: There is invisible infrastructure in the form of liberal democracy, checks and balances, courts, communities, norms.

side.boxText: Ajay Shah said this episode was built with the intellectual guidance and support of Bhargavi Zaveri-Shah, whom Amit Varma called “a very fine thinker” and who has been a guest on his podcast, *The Seen and the Unseen*. {#bhargavi}

contQuote.text: But the point is that when we give those freedoms away, it affects our security against the state. Who’s gonna protect us from the state? That is the danger. So actually we lose both.

p3.title: Tales from the paper trail
p3.deck: A man declared dead, a gangster’s laundromats, Swiss secrets and a Russian surprise

stories.start: In the village of Azamgar, in the state of Uttar Pradesh, in 1951
stories.end: Four people. That's how hard it is. That's how hard it is.
stories.caption: the man declared dead
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a man who had to prove he was alive
stories.head: Alive, but not on paper
body: Lal Bihari was born in 1951 in Azamgarh, Uttar Pradesh, Amit Varma said. In 1976 his cousins decided they wanted his land. Bribes were paid, a death certificate was produced, and at 25 Lal Bihari found he was officially dead.

If paper could make him dead, it could make him alive. He organised his own funeral and applied for compensation for his alleged widow. Then he threw stones at a police station, hoping an arrest would prove he existed.
The bribed police, Varma said, “for the first time in recorded Indian history” chose to “take a Gandhian view of the situation and ignore the stones”. {074-J02}

Next he kidnapped a 10-year-old cousin, expecting the family to come and settle matters. “There are many kids in that family, no one gives a shit,” Varma said. After ten days Lal Bihari gave the boy ice cream and sent him home. {074-J03}

He stood against VP Singh in Allahabad in 1988 and Rajiv Gandhi in Amethi in 1989, since a candidate on the rolls must be alive. He renamed himself Lal Bihari Mritak, mritak meaning dead, and founded the Uttar Pradesh Mritak Sangh. It grew to twenty thousand members, all declared dead. {#twentythousand}
In 1994 he was declared alive again. How many of the twenty thousand made it back? “Four people,” came the answer. “That’s how hard it is.” {#fourpeople}
~ We all struggle to come to terms with our mortality, Varma said. “But imagine coming to terms with your own death, which has allegedly already happened and you’re still alive.” {074-S01}
stories.why: Once the state’s paper version of a person parts from the real one, the paper wins. Four out of twenty thousand is how hard a bureaucratic record is to reverse, and it is the frame the hosts set for their talk on KYC.
stories.postscript: Behind every independent candidate who loses a deposit, Varma said, there is a story “rich in cinematic potential”. {074-J04}

stories.start: So in the good old days, banks naturally gave customers privacy
stories.end: these are the ways by which people protected themselves against governments.
stories.caption: Swiss bank secrecy
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on why Swiss bank secrecy began
stories.head: Banking on discretion
body: Banks had always kept their customers’ affairs private as an informal norm, Ajay Shah said. Then in 1933 Hitler came to power, and Nazi Germany demanded that every citizen disclose their overseas assets. No state had done that before.

Switzerland, then the banking capital of the world, feared that informal codes would not protect its foreign customers. So it passed the first laws saying that no bank would divulge information about its customers except on the order of a Swiss judge. {#swissjudge}
A German prosecutor pursuing a crime in Germany would be disregarded. “We don’t care,” Shah said, speaking for the Swiss.

~ Shah dismisses the populist noise about Swiss banks and tax havens. In the 20th century people fled their governments, he said, and a Swiss bank was one way to protect their wealth and private lives. {074-S05}

quote.text: To understand the 20th century is to see that these are the ways by which people protected themselves against governments.

stories.start: recall the interesting stories from the United States in the nineteen thirties
stories.end: you see the enforcement directorate in the newspapers, this is the problem that is
stories.caption: Al Capone’s laundromats
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on where a crime got its name
stories.head: Dirty money, clean shirts
body: In 1930s America, Ajay Shah recalled, the gangster Al Capone had a concept for his criminal cash: take it into a business with cash income, namely laundromats.

Laundromats are shops where you take your pile of clothes, stick them into a machine and collect them washed. Capone’s illicit cash was shown as the laundromat’s income. “And that’s how the word money laundering emerged,” Shah said. {074-S04}
“We are all in this mess,” Shah said, “because governments want to go block this kind of money laundering.” From that effort grew a worldwide system of financial surveillance.
~ Every time the Enforcement Directorate appears in the newspapers, Shah said, this is the problem at work. {#edpapers}
stories.why: The crime that now justifies watching everyone’s money began as one gangster’s cover story. In Shah’s telling, every Enforcement Directorate headline is a consequence of states trying to block that trick.

stories.start: I have a good friend who is an official who got private, quiet conversations
stories.end: They didn't know how to do it by themselves.
stories.caption: the Russian officials’ surprise
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on an official’s talk with Russian counterparts
stories.head: From Washington, with lessons
body: A good friend of Ajay Shah’s, an Indian official, once had private, quiet conversations with Russian counterparts. They told him something, Shah said, with a great sense of wonder.
“Did you know the American Treasury is teaching us how to oppress our own people?” {074-S06}
The US Treasury, Shah explained, had taught the Russian government how to build a mass surveillance system in finance. The Russians, he said, had not known how to do it by themselves.

~ For Shah, this was where the American push against money laundering and terror finance after the 9/11 attacks had led. The whole story, he said, “is really a blot” on the conscience of the United States. {#blot}
stories.why: Tools built against terror can be turned on citizens. A system made in the name of following terrorists’ money, Shah argued, handed the Russian government the know-how to watch its own people.

quiz.q: Why did Lal Bihari throw stones at a police station in Uttar Pradesh?
quiz.a: He hoped to be arrested, because an arrest would prove he existed.

quiz.q: Where does the term ‘money laundering’ come from, according to Ajay Shah?
quiz.a: Al Capone’s laundromats, where criminal cash was shown as the laundromat’s income.

quiz.q: What did Switzerland do in response to Nazi Germany’s 1933 law on overseas assets?
quiz.a: It made bank secrecy law: only a Swiss judge could order disclosure.

quiz.q: How, in Ajay Shah’s counterexample, can $100,000 be moved past X-ray machines?
quiz.a: A 555 cigarette box packed with diamonds, invisible to X-ray machines.

quiz.q: What is Ajay Shah’s general law about technology and a malfunctioning Indian government?
quiz.a: Adding CPUs never makes it better: CPUs are never the answer.

quiz.q: Which song did Amit Varma pick, and to whom did Ajay Shah suggest sending it?
quiz.a: *Every Breath You Take* by The Police, to all the civil servants in your life.
